title: Darjeeling tea: a history from 1835 to your cup
meta_description: How the 1835 Deed of Grant, Campbell's 1841 seeds and Nepali labour built Darjeeling tea, what the flushes mean, and how to visit a garden and buy well.
summary: Darjeeling tea began with a land grant in 1835, a superintendent's garden experiment in 1841 and commercial gardens from 1852, worked largely by migrants from Nepal. Today about 87 gardens make under 1 percent of India's tea, protected since 2004 by India's first Geographical Indication. Visit March to June to see plucking and taste the flushes.

sections.heading: A hill handed over: the 1835 Deed of Grant
paras: Tea in Darjeeling starts with a land deal. In 1828–29 two British officers, Captain George Lloyd and J. W. Grant, passing through to settle a border dispute between Sikkim and Nepal, stayed at the ridge then called Dorje Ling and saw a healthy site for a sanatorium. The East India Company pressed the Chogyal of Sikkim, Tsugphud Namgyal, for it. On 1 February 1835 he signed a Deed of Grant handing over the Darjeeling hill tract, a strip of about 138 square miles, to the Company.

The deed was short and asked for nothing in return, but from 1841 the Company paid the Chogyal an annual allowance of Rs 3,000, raised to Rs 6,000 in 1846. Relations soured after Sikkim detained the botanist Joseph Hooker and the superintendent Archibald Campbell in 1849, and in 1850 the British annexed the Terai and a much larger block of hills. Kalimpong was taken from Bhutan by the Treaty of Sinchula in 1865. The district map we know today was largely complete by 1866.

sections.heading: Campbell's garden and the first estates
paras: Archibald Campbell, a doctor posted as Darjeeling's first superintendent in 1839, planted tea seeds in his garden at Beechwood in 1841. The seeds were of the China type, raised in Kumaon in the western Himalaya. They grew well in the cool, misty air and the steep, well-drained slopes, and others followed with experimental plots at Lebong and elsewhere.

Around the same time the plant hunter Robert Fortune was collecting tea plants and seed in China for the Company between 1848 and 1851, and some of his stock is said to have reached the Darjeeling nurseries. The government began offering land for tea, and the first commercial gardens, among them Tukvar, Steinthal and Aloobari, opened from 1852. Happy Valley, just below the town, dates from the 1850s. By the 1870s there were more than a hundred gardens, and the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway was built in 1879–81 in large part to carry their tea down to the plains.

sections.heading: The people who made it
paras: The gardens needed thousands of workers, and the forests of the district were thinly peopled. Planters recruited labour mainly from eastern Nepal, and whole families came: Rai, Limbu, Tamang, Gurung, Magar and many others, who together formed the Nepali-speaking Gorkha community that is now the majority in the hills. Lepcha and Bhutia families, the older inhabitants, also worked on and around the estates.

Life on a garden was hard and closely controlled. Workers lived in garden lines, were paid partly in rations, and depended on the estate for housing, water and medical care. The Plantation Labour Act of 1951 set rules for housing, health and welfare that still shape the gardens. Wages and land rights remain live issues, and the history of tea labour sits close to the heart of the Gorkhaland movement. In 2017 a 104-day shutdown during the agitation stopped plucking through most of the second-flush and monsoon seasons.

sections.heading: Flushes, grades and what is in the cup
paras: Darjeeling tea is plucked as two leaves and a bud, by hand, from bushes that are mostly the China variety and newer clonal cultivars such as AV2. It is made by the orthodox method: the leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised, dried and sorted, never cut by the CTC machines used for most Indian tea. The year is divided into flushes, the growth spurts that follow rest or rain.

Grades on the label describe leaf size and quality, not taste. FTGFOP means Finest Tippy Golden Flowery Orange Pekoe, a whole-leaf tea with many golden tips; an added S for Special or a 1 marks the best lots. More useful is the garden name, the flush and the invoice or lot number, which tell you exactly where and when the tea was made.

sections.heading: Protecting the Darjeeling name
paras: For decades far more tea was sold as Darjeeling around the world than the hills could ever grow. The Tea Board of India fought back with a certification logo, a woman holding two leaves and a bud, and in 2004 Darjeeling tea became the first product in India to receive a Geographical Indication, the legal protection that ties a name to a place. The European Union later registered it as a protected geographical indication too.

Only tea grown and processed in the registered gardens of the Darjeeling hill areas may now use the name. Output has fallen in recent decades because of old bushes, climate stress, labour shortages and the 2017 shutdown, and it is now well under 10 million kg a year, less than 1 percent of India's tea. That scarcity is part of why a good first flush costs what it does.

sections.heading: Visiting a garden: what to expect
paras: Tea gardens are workplaces, not parks, and each estate sets its own rules for visitors. Several welcome guests for walks and tastings, and a few run homestays or bungalows. Go on a working morning, Monday to Saturday, between March and November, when pluckers are on the slopes and the factory is processing. From December to February the bushes are dormant and factories rest.
list: Happy Valley Tea Estate, a 3 km walk below Chowrasta: garden walk and, in season, a look at the factory; ₹100–300, indicative 2026.
Makaibari, below Kurseong: garden walks and tastings, ₹200–500; one of the best-known estates in the hills.
The gardens around Mirik, such as Thurbo, Okayti and Gopaldhara, seen from the road on the drive from Darjeeling.
Glenburn, above the Rangeet river: a working estate with planters' bungalows for overnight guests, from about ₹35,000 a suite night with meals, indicative.
Tea tasting rooms near Chowrasta and on Nehru Road, where you can compare flushes and gardens by the cup for ₹80–250.

sections.heading: Buying tea without being fooled
paras: Buy from a shop that lets you taste and that writes the garden, flush and year on the packet. A 100 g pack of a named garden's first flush costs roughly ₹400–1,500, indicative 2026, and the finest lots far more. Loose tea in big sacks at low prices labelled simply Darjeeling is usually blended with tea from the plains or Nepal.

Look for the Darjeeling logo on branded packs. Buy small quantities of two or three teas rather than a kilo of one, since Darjeeling tea loses its fragrance within a year. Store it in an airtight tin away from light. Brew first flush with water just off the boil, about 85–90 °C, for 3 minutes, and drink it without milk: that is how the planters and the tasters drink it, and it is the only way to find the flavour you paid for.

faqs.q: When did tea growing start in Darjeeling
faqs.a: In 1841, when Archibald Campbell, the first superintendent, planted China-type tea seeds in his garden at Beechwood. The plants did well, and the government began granting land for tea. The first commercial gardens, including Tukvar, Steinthal and Aloobari, opened from 1852. By the 1870s there were more than a hundred.

faqs.q: What was the 1835 Deed of Grant
faqs.a: A deed signed on 1 February 1835 by Tsugphud Namgyal, the Chogyal of Sikkim, handing over the Darjeeling hill tract to the East India Company as a sanatorium. From 1841 the Company paid him an annual allowance. After relations broke down in 1849, the British annexed much more land in 1850, shaping today's district.

faqs.q: How many tea gardens are there in Darjeeling
faqs.a: About 87 gardens are registered to produce Darjeeling tea, spread across the Darjeeling, Kurseong and Mirik areas and the valleys below them. Some are large estates with their own factories; a few smaller growers sell leaf to bigger gardens. The exact number shifts slightly as gardens close, merge or reopen.

First flush is the first plucking of the year, from late February to April, after the bushes rest through winter. The young leaves make a light, pale, floral tea with a green-gold colour. It is the most sought-after Darjeeling and usually the most expensive. Second flush follows in May and June.

faqs.q: What is the muscatel flavour in Darjeeling tea
faqs.a: Muscatel describes a fruity, grape-like note found in some second-flush Darjeeling teas, plucked in May and June. It is linked to the season's growth and, in part, to small insects that feed on the leaves and change their chemistry. Not every second flush has it, which is why the best lots fetch high prices.

Because there is so little of it. The hills produce well under 10 million kg a year, less than 1 percent of India's tea, from old bushes on steep slopes that must be plucked by hand. Yields are low, labour costs are high, and global demand is strong. The GI protection keeps blended teas from using the name.

faqs.q: Can we visit a tea factory in Darjeeling
faqs.a: Yes, at some gardens. Happy Valley, close to town, and Makaibari, below Kurseong, usually welcome visitors for walks and tastings, and their factories can be seen when processing is under way, roughly March to November. Visits depend on each estate's rules and are often closed on Sundays. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Who works on Darjeeling's tea gardens
faqs.a: Mostly Nepali-speaking families whose ancestors were recruited from eastern Nepal from the 1850s onwards, along with Lepcha and Bhutia families. Many workers, especially pluckers, are women. Garden communities have lived on the same estates for generations, and their wages and land rights remain important political issues in the hills.

faqs.q: How should I brew Darjeeling tea
faqs.a: Use about 2–3 g of leaf per cup, water just off the boil at about 85–90 °C for first flush and nearer boiling for second and autumn flush, and steep for 3–4 minutes. Drink it without milk or sugar to taste the flavour. Over-steeping or boiling water makes it bitter.
